task: A9.9 aggressive but honest UNSW attack-family improvement strategy design
current_accepted_baseline: A9 linear Head 2 hierarchical UNSW baseline
a9_6_lesson: Simply increasing Head 2 loss pressure from attack_loss_weight 1.0 to 1.5 was not enough and hurt attack-family or rare-class quality.
a9_7_lesson: Changing Head 2 from linear to an MLP branch provided some signal but failed single-run replacement.
a9_8_lesson: Formal multi-seed comparison showed A9.7 branch was slightly better on average but not enough for promotion; simple branch capacity should not be the next major UNSW direction.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Keep A9 Head 1 as binary router and train a separate attack-only classifier for attack-family prediction.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Highest chance of meaningful attack-family macro-F1 improvement while preserving a clean hierarchical IDS story.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Train shared model normally, then freeze or partially freeze encoder and fine-tune attack-family branch on attack rows.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Potentially useful backup, but attribution and overfitting risks are higher than a separate specialist.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Use train-only attack-family sampling or class-aware batching to improve minority-family exposure.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Useful as part of specialist training, but weaker and riskier as a standalone experiment.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Apply focal loss to Head 2 attack-family learning.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Not recommended as the next major experiment because A9.6 already showed loss pressure alone can be unsafe.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Add auxiliary hard-class heads or one-vs-rest specialists for Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Shellcode, and Worms.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Potentially useful diagnostically, but too complex and messy for the next controlled professor-facing step.

strategies_evaluated.summary: Add categorical or interaction features using train-fitted transforms only.
strategies_evaluated.assessment: Possible future direction, but late-stage leakage and reproducibility risk make it less suitable than the specialist.

strategy_ranking.reason: Best balance of expected attack-family macro-F1 improvement, rare-class protection, clean hierarchy, and professor-facing clarity.
Reasonable backup but harder to explain and more prone to overfitting or attribution ambiguity.
Useful inside the specialist protocol but not strong enough as the main standalone strategy.
Loss-only change is less compelling after A9.6 and may worsen rare-class precision.
Could become too complex with too many competing models and unclear professor-facing presentation.
Potentially useful but higher leakage and reproducibility burden this late.

why_recommended: It directly targets attack-family boundaries instead of adding another small loss or capacity tweak.
It keeps A9 Head 1 fixed, protecting the accepted binary detector.
It matches the hierarchical IDS story: binary detector routes detected attacks into an attack-family specialist.
It can use train-only attack-row sampling without contaminating the binary detector.
It separates routed end-to-end performance from oracle attack-row diagnostic performance.
why_stronger_than_focal_loss_alone: Focal loss alone changes the loss shape but leaves the mixed hierarchical training problem intact. The specialist removes benign-vs-attack pressure from the attack-family learner, focuses capacity on attack-family boundaries, and can use train-only sampling while preserving A9 Head 1.
why_stronger_than_head2_branch_capacity: A9.7 and A9.8 showed simple Head 2 branch capacity only produced a small attack-family macro-F1 mean gain of +0.004524. The specialist changes the task decomposition and training distribution rather than merely increasing branch size.

realistic_target_range.rare_class_macro_f1: protect A9/A9.8 range and seek modest improvement
realistic_target_range.binary_macro_f1: remain close to A9 because A9 Head 1 is unchanged

unrealistic_claims_rejected: Do not claim attack-family macro-F1 above 0.9 is realistic for this corrected UNSW setup.
Do not claim the specialist works before training and evaluation.
Do not claim focal loss, branch capacity, or sampling will solve rare classes without controlled validation.
professor_facing_story: A secure hierarchical IDS first detects whether traffic is benign or attack. Detected attacks are then routed to a dedicated attack-family specialist trained only to separate attack families.
leakage_controls: Train specialist only on UNSW training attack rows.
Compute any class weights or sampling probabilities from training attack labels only.
Use validation attack rows only for selection and optional calibration.
Use test labels only once after all choices are frozen.
Do not use validation or test labels for sampling, weights, or preprocessing decisions.
Keep A9 Head 1 fixed for specialist-only evaluation.
Report routed and oracle attack-row metrics separately.
test_tuning_controls: Predefine promotion criteria before final test evaluation.
Use validation metrics for model selection and calibration.
Do not repeat test evaluation to choose hyperparameters.
Record all planned artifact paths and commands before training.
expected_risks: Specialist overfitting because attack-only training has fewer rows.
Class-balanced sampling may distort class priors or calibration.
End-to-end routed performance remains limited by A9 Head 1 false negatives.
Routed and oracle attack-row metrics can be confused if documentation is careless.
Additional specialist artifact adds model-management complexity.
main_review_decision_needed_next: Approve or reject A9.9-prep for the attack-family specialist strategy. Approval should be for preparation only first, not immediate training.
